Title: 30-m Landsat Cropland Mapping of Australia and China on Google Earth Engine
Authors: Teluguntla, R., M. B. Anderson, W. W. Tschudi, A. W. C. Huete, and C. J. Kucharik
Journal: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing, 2018, Vol. 142, pp. 87-101
DOI: 10.1016/j.isprsjprs.2018.05.006
URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isprsjprs.2018.05.006

Part: Introduction (about 80 words)
- 2018 study, Teluguntla and colleagues, ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
- Made high-accuracy 30-meter cropland extent maps for Australia and China
- Used Landsat-8, random forest classifier, Google Earth Engine (GEE)
- Results matter, but method is the bigger story
- Shows continent-scale, field-level mapping is practical, repeatable, affordable

Part: Why Australia and China? (about 50 words)
- China: huge population, comparatively small farmland area, fragmented intensively managed plots
- Australia: vast sparsely populated farm regions, large fields, dryland farming, irrigation in particular basins
- If one approach maps both well, good sign it travels to other regions
- That was the study's central bet

Part: Why 30 meters matters (about 100 words)
- Earlier global land cover products used 250 m to 1 km imagery
- One pixel mixes crops, fallow land, trees, roads, buildings
- Small-field places like much of China: cropland extent hard to pin down
- Landsat-8: 30-meter pixels, resolve individual fields in many areas
- Temporal dimension crucial: cropland defined by what it does over time as much as how it looks on one date

Part: The method in brief (about 40 words)
- Time-series imagery: multiple Landsat-8 observations, not one cloud-free scene
- Composited into summaries of seasonal vegetation patterns; cropland's rise and fall in greenness informs classifier

Part: Google Earth Engine as enabler (about 90 words)
- Traditionally: download terabytes, store locally, preprocess, heavy computation on dedicated hardware
- Barrier kept many teams from attempting the work
- Write analysis once, run over huge areas without moving data
- Makes approach scalable: same code for another region with little change, results refreshed as new imagery arrives

Part: Why random forest fits (about 30 words)
- Valuable for large-area mapping: predictable across very different landscapes, easier to scale than per-region recalibration

Part: The method in brief (about 40 words)
- Training and validation samples: cropland/non-cropland reference data, used to train and separately to test
- Independent sets essential for honest accuracy estimate

Part: Strengths and caveats (about 60 words)
- Binary map doesn't say which crops, whether irrigated, or how intensively farmed
- Supervised classification quality depends on quality and spatial coverage of reference samples, costly over large areas

Part: Food and water security (about 70 words)
- Cropland footprint helps estimate irrigation demand, pressure on river basins and aquifers, target water management
- Especially relevant: Australia (water allocation constant concern), northern China (serious groundwater depletion)
- Consistent method allows comparisons national datasets with differing definitions and standards often cannot

The border collie is a medium-sized herding dog that originated on the Scottish border. It was bred to herd livestock, primarily sheep. It has an intense gaze that allows it to control flock movement. It is a hard worker and can run tirelessly all day long.

Title: The Border Collie: From Drover's Dog to Herding Prodigy

Part: Opening: Herding Miracle (about 60 words)
- Dog drops low, locks eyes on flock, quiet intensity like chess player three moves ahead
- No barking, no chaos; stare, slow arc around sheep, flock goes exactly where asked

Part: The Eye, the Stalk, the Brain (about 110 words)
- These = modified predatory sequence of wolves and other canids: orient, eye, stalk, chase
- In border collies grab-and-kill end largely bred out; early steps run with extraordinary refinement
- The eye: intense fixed stare pressuring livestock without contact
- The stalk: low deliberate approach, moves sheep by presence not force
- Responsiveness: unusual willingness to take handler direction, even at distance

Part: Rugged Beginnings on the Border (about 50 words)
- Selection brutally practical; not breeding for ribbons, breeding a dog to bring flock home
- Dogs that thought independently, endured bad weather, read animal movement earned keep and passed on traits

Part: Adam Telfer and Foundation (about 60 words)
- Adam Telfer, Northumberland shepherd, 19th century; often credited with consolidating the type via deliberate crossbreeding, strengthening wanted working qualities
- Telfer's contribution not a look but fixing working traits so they reappear each generation

Part: Working Over Looks (about 110 words)
- Heart of breed's identity: unlike show-ring-standard breeds, shaped by working-over-looks ethos; herded = bred, couldn't = appearance didn't save it
- Black and white classic; merles, reds, tricolors and others too; variety = fingerprint of breeders caring about ability above all
- Sheepdog trials, begun 19th century, still popular; reinforced focus; let shepherds compare dogs side by side, rewarding calm, efficient stock movement under pressure

Part: The Flip Side: Demanding Temperament (about 120 words)
- Admiration needs realism; traits brilliant in pasture can be difficult in typical home
- Behaviorist Patricia McConnell, writes on herding breeds, herded with her own border collies: dogs bred to work, drive doesn't switch off in a house
- Dog built to control moving things may fixate on cars, bicycles, joggers, children
- Practical signs: nipping heels or herding family, esp. kids
- Dog built to think all day invents its own jobs if none given; you may not like them

Part: Is It Right for You? (about 30 words)
- Needs real mental work: training, puzzles, structured games, dog sports (agility, flyball), ideally actual herding

Part: A Breed Made by Work (about 30 words)
- Give it a job and it astonishes; leave it without one and it finds its own

Title: Diocese of Richmond Consensus Curriculum: Forming the Whole Student
- The Diocese of Richmond in Virginia has begun implementing its Consensus Curriculum, which aims to form the whole student through faith at the center, not on the side
- The curriculum is built around four intellectual goals: rigorous academic instruction, intellectual humility, respect for truth, and an authentic sense of self-worth
- Teachers can refer to the Diocese of Richmond Consensus Curriculum Handbook, which offers suggestions for integrating these goals into their lessons
- The curriculum is not intended to be a substitute for academic excellence, but rather a way to enhance it by providing a framework for students to consider the moral implications of their academic work
- It is designed to be used across all grades and subjects, and teachers are encouraged to find natural, honest connections between faith and academic content
- The curriculum is also intended to be a guide for principals, who are responsible for ensuring its effective implementation
- They should observe classrooms, support teacher growth, review student progress, and see that standards are being met
- The curriculum is a consensus among the diocese's schools, which means that students who move between diocesan Catholic schools will be able to transition smoothly
- However, individual schools are still free to tailor the curriculum to meet the needs of their own communities
- One distinctive component of the curriculum is the Benziger Family Life Series, which aims to help students understand human growth, relationships, and family life from a Catholic perspective
- The Church teaches that parents are the primary educators of their children, and the curriculum aims to support parents rather than replace them
- It is important to note that the curriculum is intended for Catholic schools only, and that families should check with their schools about how they handle questions about the content of the program

Part 1: rechargeable batteries (about 60 words)
- Modern "low self-discharge" versions hold charge for months in drawer; fine for low-drain devices
- Financial: higher upfront cost, often pays for itself after a handful of charges in frequently used devices; then recharges cost pennies
- Environmental: one rechargeable reused hundreds of times, replaces pile of disposables

Part 2: Commercial Car Wash (about 140 words)
- Surprising: washing at home feels thrifty and harmless but often isn't good for environment
- Many areas: storm drains carry runoff untreated to streams, rivers, lakes
- Driveway wash: water, soap, brake dust, oil, road grime run into storm drain
- Running garden hose can use more water than expected
- Environmental: commercial washes generally required to send wastewater to treatment, not storm drains; many use high-pressure, low-volume equipment and water reclamation, much less fresh water per car
- Swap: professional car wash, ideally one that recycles water

Part 3: Reusable Cleaning Supplies (about 60 words)
- Financial: pack of microfiber cloths costs about same as a few rolls of paper towels, lasts years; concentrates much cheaper per use than ready-to-use bottles
- Tip: small basket for used cloths under sink, launder with regular wash; keep paper towels for truly messy jobs; goal is to cut back, not be perfect

Part 4: Local, Seasonal Food (about 140 words)
- Honest caveat: transportation usually smaller share of food's footprint than how it's produced
- Environmental: fresher produce lasts longer at home, less food waste; food waste among biggest household contributors to greenhouse gas emissions
- Still, local/seasonal often means less packaging, less refrigerated storage, less spoilage before reaching you; supports local farms
- Financial: in-season produce often cheaper because plentiful; longer-lasting food means fewer wasted dollars
- Tip: start with one weekly item (eggs, apples, tomatoes in summer) bought locally; build from there

Part 5: LED Light Bulbs (about 140 words)
- Financial: LEDs cost 3-5 times as much as traditional bulbs; last 25 times longer and use 75% less energy
- Environmental: LEDs use less energy, produce less heat, contain no mercury, and burn out less often, all good for planet and wallet
- Swap: LED bulbs, ideally those labeled "Energy Star"; can use "lighting calculator" to figure out how much you'll save

This case illustrates the four functions of a physical distribution center. The primary functions are to: (1) receive goods; (2) store goods; (3) pick goods; and (4) ship goods. The case also illustrates the importance of considering information, particularly data, in evaluating the cost and benefits of a distribution center.

In this case, the non-profit agency was receiving goods directly from the supplier and storing the goods in their facility before picking and shipping the goods to the agencies. The non-profit was acting as a distribution center, but not adding value to the supply chain. In fact, the distribution center was adding costs to the supply chain. The agency was not receiving any benefit from the distribution center that was worth the costs.

The non-profit agency had to decide whether to continue to use their distribution center or eliminate the distribution center. To make this decision, the agency should have considered whether their distribution center was adding value to their supply chain by performing one of the four physical functions or providing information. In this case, the distribution center was not performing any of the four physical functions, and the non-profit agency could get all the information they needed without a distribution center.

The non-profit agency decided to eliminate their distribution center and have the suppliers ship the goods directly to the agencies. This decision eliminated costs from their supply chain and improved their efficiency. The non-profit agency was able to focus on their core business of providing services to their clients.

When considering whether to use a distribution center, it is important to consider the four physical functions and the information that the distribution center can provide. If the distribution center is not adding value to the supply chain, then it should be eliminated.

High blood pressure is called the silent killer for a reason. It often has no symptoms, and if untreated, it can lead to serious health problems like heart attacks and strokes. That’s why it’s important to have your blood pressure checked regularly. But just getting a single reading at your doctor’s office isn’t enough. 

The problem is that a single reading doesn’t tell the whole story. It’s just a snapshot, taken in a highly controlled environment and after you’ve been waiting in a doctor’s office, which is inherently stressful. A single reading doesn’t show how your blood pressure varies throughout the day. And because blood pressure fluctuates all the time, it’s important to get an accurate measure of your overall average. 

That’s why experts recommend monitoring your blood pressure at home. Home monitoring shows the bigger picture: your normal, everyday blood pressure readings when you’re not under stress. In fact, the American Heart Association (AHA) recommends home monitoring for anyone diagnosed with high blood pressure. And they recommend it for anyone whose blood pressure is considered elevated, which means it’s higher than normal but not high enough for a diagnosis of high blood pressure. 

Home monitoring can also be helpful for people who have normal blood pressure. That’s because even people with normal blood pressure can develop high blood pressure as they get older. And high blood pressure increases the risk of heart disease and stroke. If you have any of the risk factors for high blood pressure, including a family history of high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, or kidney disease, your doctor may recommend monitoring your blood pressure at home. 

How often should you check your blood pressure at home? 

The AHA recommends that people with high blood pressure check their blood pressure at home at least once a day, over the course of a week, before their appointment with their doctor. They recommend checking your blood pressure twice a day—morning and evening—taking two readings each time, one minute apart. 

Many guidelines recommend discarding the first reading of the day and averaging the remaining readings. 

Once your blood pressure is under control, you may be able to cut back on your home monitoring. Many experts recommend checking your blood pressure at home a few times a week, or once a month. Your doctor can advise you on how often you should check your blood pressure at home. 

If you don’t have high blood pressure but you have any of the risk factors for high blood pressure, or you’re over 40 years old, it’s a good idea to monitor your blood pressure at home occasionally. That way, you’ll know if you develop high blood pressure and can seek treatment early. 

How often should you check your blood pressure at home if you don’t have high blood pressure or any risk factors? 

Experts recommend checking your blood pressure at home occasionally, if you’re over 40 years old or have any of the risk factors for high blood pressure. You could do a week of readings every few months, or whenever you have a clinic reading that’s high. 

You could also check your blood pressure at home a few times a week, especially if you have any of the risk factors for high blood pressure. 

It’s a good idea to check your blood pressure at home when you feel ill, or if you’ve been very active or inactive, or if you’ve been eating a lot of salt. 

Why is it important to check your blood pressure at home at the same time each day? 

Checking your blood pressure at the same time each day makes it easier to compare your readings. It also gives you a better idea of how your blood pressure fluctuates throughout the day. 

The best time to check your blood pressure is in the morning, within an hour of waking up. That’s because blood pressure tends to surge in the morning. This morning surge is linked to heart attacks and strokes, so morning readings are especially valuable. 

When you’re checking your blood pressure at home, make sure you’re consistent about the time of day. 

How should you take a blood pressure reading at home? 

To get an accurate reading at home, it’s important to use the right technique. 

1. Rest first: sit quietly for at least five minutes before you take your blood pressure. Don’t talk, scroll on your phone, or watch anything stressful. 

2. Empty your bladder: a full bladder can raise your blood pressure reading. 

3. Avoid coffee, cigarettes, and exercise: don’t drink coffee, smoke, or exercise for at least 30 minutes before taking your blood pressure. 

4. Check the cuff size: using a cuff that’s too small can lead to falsely high readings, while using a cuff that’s too large can lead to falsely low readings. 

5. Position the cuff on bare skin: make sure the cuff is on bare skin, not over clothing. 

6. Place the cuff on the same arm each time, and make sure the arm is at heart level. 

7. Sit with your back supported and your feet flat on the floor. 

8. Relax your arm on a table with your palm up. Don’t cross your legs or dangle your feet. 

9. Don’t talk while you’re taking your blood pressure. 

10. Take two readings, one minute apart, and average the readings. 

11. Make sure you’re using a validated monitor: automatic upper-arm monitors are generally more accurate than wrist or finger devices. 

12. Choose a clinically validated device: make sure the device you use has been clinically validated. Many devices claim to be clinically validated, but they may not be. 

It’s a good idea to bring your home monitor to your doctor’s office so you can compare the readings from your home monitor to the readings from your doctor’s equipment. 

What do your blood pressure numbers mean? 

Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg) and recorded as two numbers: systolic pressure (the top number) and diastolic pressure (the bottom number). 

For example, if your systolic pressure is 120 and your diastolic pressure is 80, you would write your blood pressure as 120/80 mm Hg. 

What do the numbers mean? 

Systolic pressure (the top number): the pressure in your blood vessels when your heart beats. 

Diastolic pressure (the bottom number): the pressure in your blood vessels when your heart rests between beats. 

What do the numbers mean for you? 

Normal blood pressure: less than 120/80 mm Hg 

Elevated blood pressure: systolic between 120–129 and diastolic less than 80 

Stage 1 high blood pressure: systolic 130–139 or diastolic 80–89 

Stage 2 high blood pressure: systolic 140 or higher or diastolic 90 or higher 

Hypertensive crisis (emergency care required): systolic 180 or higher or diastolic 120 or higher 

If you have high blood pressure, your doctor will recommend a treatment plan based on your health and your blood pressure numbers. 

The goal of treatment is to lower your blood pressure to below 140/90 mm Hg. For some people, the goal is an even lower blood pressure. 

What if your blood pressure is very high? 

If your blood pressure is very high, seek medical attention right away. A very high blood pressure reading can be a sign of a hypertensive crisis, which is an emergency. 

What are the symptoms of a hypertensive crisis? 

A hypertensive crisis can cause: 

- Chest pain 

- Shortness of breath 

- Severe headache 

- Vision changes 

- Difficulty speaking 

- Numbness or weakness 

- Confusion 

If you have any of these symptoms, call 911 or go to your nearest emergency department. 

What if your blood pressure is very low? 

A very low blood pressure reading can be a sign of a medical emergency, especially if you have symptoms like: 

- Confusion 

- Dizziness or lightheadedness 

- Fainting 

- Blurred vision 

- Nausea

This article discusses the differences between tort and contract law, with particular emphasis on the liability of businesses for harms caused by their products. A key aspect of tort law is its "duty of care," whereby a person has an obligation to act reasonably in order to avoid harming others. In contrast, contract law requires a party to perform a specific duty as set forth in an agreement. The article describes the consequences of committing an intentional tort, which may include punitive damages, versus an unintentional tort, which typically results in only compensatory damages. Additionally, the article provides examples of common torts such as negligence and defamation, as well as the distinction between strict liability and products liability. Finally, the article outlines common defenses available to defendants in tort cases.

Discussion Questions:
1. What are some examples of intentional torts that might arise in a business context?
2. How does the "duty of care" apply to businesses?
3. What are some ways that businesses can limit their exposure to liability for injuries caused by their products?
4. Under what circumstances might a business be liable for injuries caused by a third party's use of its product?

Answer to Discussion Question 1: Examples of intentional torts that might arise in a business context include assault, battery, false imprisonment, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. These types of torts often occur when an employee of a business acts outside of his or her authority or commits an act of violence against a customer or coworker.

Answer to Discussion Question 2: The "duty of care" applies to businesses in various ways, depending on the nature of their operations. For example, businesses that manufacture products have a duty to ensure that those products are safe for consumers to use. Businesses that provide services also have a duty to ensure that they do not negligently cause harm to their customers. Additionally, businesses have a duty to protect the privacy of customer data and to take reasonable steps to prevent data breaches.

Answer to Discussion Question 3: Some ways that businesses can limit their exposure to liability for injuries caused by their products include conducting thorough testing and safety inspections, obtaining adequate insurance coverage, and providing clear instructions and warnings regarding the proper use of the product. Businesses can also limit their exposure by ensuring that their employees are properly trained and supervised.

Answer to Discussion Question 4: A business might be liable for injuries caused by a third party's use of its product if the business had a duty to prevent the injury from occurring. For example, if a business sold a defective product to a distributor, who then sold it to a consumer, the business might be liable if the consumer was injured by the product. Another example would be if a business failed to take reasonable steps to ensure the safety of its premises, and a third party was injured as a result.

Key Takeaways:
- The primary distinction between tort and contract law is that contract law focuses on agreements between parties, while tort law addresses harms caused by one party to another.
- Intentional torts involve deliberate actions that cause harm, whereas unintentional torts result from negligence or other forms of carelessness.
- Strict liability is a form of liability that exists regardless of whether a party exercised reasonable care in avoiding the harm.
- Products liability refers to liability for harms caused by defective products, including manufacturing defects, design defects, and failure to warn about known risks.

This summer, the Texas Legislature is facing a question: Should it reauthorize a task force created to study why mothers die in childbirth?

The answer is yes, but the task force, now set to expire on Sept. 1, should be reauthorized for just a year, with a plan to return it to the Legislature next spring for a full review of what comes next.

When the Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force was created in 2013, it was to investigate a crisis: Texas had the highest maternal mortality rate in the developed world. A 2013 study found that nearly 50 women per 100,000 births died in Texas, compared with an average of 12 women per 100,000 in other high-income countries.

That’s a problem for a state that prides itself on having the best health care in the world.

As the task force was working, the data got worse. The state Department of State Health Services released a report in 2016 saying that the death rate had increased to 57 women per 100,000 live births. The data is still under review, and the death rate could fall when it’s finalized. But even the lower number is staggering.

The task force’s work has been crucial in sorting out the causes of these deaths. It has brought together physicians, nurses, epidemiologists, public health experts and maternal health experts to review the deaths case by case. It has helped identify problems with how the state records maternal deaths, including how pregnancy is recorded on death certificates and how the data is coded. Some of the deaths previously reported as maternal deaths were reclassified as cardiac arrests, for example, or overdoses.

The task force is working to correct these data problems, but its work is far from finished. Because of the data problems, many of the deaths that occurred during the time the task force has been working have yet to be fully reviewed. The task force’s work has already uncovered preventable causes of death. And the task force has identified areas that need more research, including the racial disparities in maternal mortality.

The task force has recommended several important changes, including a plan to provide free long-acting birth control to any woman who requests it. But there are many more things that need to be done to prevent deaths, including expanding Medicaid coverage to more pregnant women, ensuring that women have access to substance abuse treatment and mental health care, and expanding access to health care in rural areas.

The task force has been working since 2013. The Legislature should extend it for another year, giving lawmakers a chance to decide whether they want to continue funding the task force. But they should also take the recommendations of the task force to heart and act on them.

This summer, the Legislature will have a chance to do the easy thing — pass an extension for the task force. But lawmakers will also have a chance to do the hard thing and act on what the task force has uncovered. That would make a real difference in the lives of Texas mothers.

This is an article about financial bubbles and their impact on the stock market. A financial bubble occurs when the price of an asset rises far beyond what underlying value justifies. This happens because the buyers expect the prices to climb, not because the underlying value is increasing. As buyers keep buying and the prices keep climbing, more and more people join in. Eventually, buyers run out of money or confidence, and prices fall. This sudden fall is called the "burst." Financial bubbles are especially dangerous because debt magnifies losses. For example, if a house is bought with borrowed money, and the price falls, the borrower might not be able to repay the loan. Lenders then pull back, forcing sellers to lower their prices even further. When this happens, money flows into other assets, causing their prices to rise. This can create a chain reaction, dragging down the entire market.

A market bubble refers to a situation where the stock prices of a particular sector or the entire stock market rise far beyond what underlying fundamentals justify. A classic example is the dot-com bubble in the late 1990s, when technology companies with little or no profits saw their stock prices soar. The Nasdaq Composite Index, which tracks the tech sector, peaked in March 2009 and lost roughly three-quarters of its value over the next two years. It took more than 15 years for the Nasdaq to recover to its pre-bubble level.

An economic bubble happens when the prices of goods and services in a particular sector or the entire economy rise far beyond what underlying fundamentals justify. The classic example is Japan in the late 1980s, when the stock and real estate markets soared to record levels. Both markets collapsed in the early 1990s, leading to a decade of economic stagnation. The Nikkei stock index peaked at the end of 1989 and did not return to its pre-bubble level for more than 30 years.

For new investors, it's essential to learn about bubbles and their warning signs. While no one can predict a crash perfectly, certain patterns tend to repeat themselves. If prices are far above fundamentals, such as price-to-earnings ratios, it's a good idea to be skeptical. Easy credit, weak or nonexistent profits, and fear of missing out are also warning signs. By understanding these patterns, new investors can protect themselves from the dangers of financial bubbles.
